stem: In ancient India, the traditional residential system of education in which students lived with their teacher (guru) in his home/hermitage, receiving free education in exchange for household duties and service, was known as the:
explanation: The Gurukul system centred education around a close, residential guru-shishya (teacher-student) relationship, with students serving the guru's household while receiving oral instruction — distinct from the later Madrasa system (Islamic education) or the colonial-era Monitorial (Bell-Lancaster) system, where senior pupils taught junior ones.

stem: This ancient centre of Buddhist learning in present-day Bihar, considered one of the world's first residential international universities, attracted scholars from as far as China and Tibet before being destroyed in the 12th century. It was:
explanation: Nalanda (Bihar) was a globally renowned residential Buddhist university, drawing scholars like Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) from China — Takshashila (in present-day Pakistan) was an earlier, equally famous centre of learning, but was not primarily Buddhist-monastic in the same residential-university sense.
